response.translation: For where our task is to fill a sinus with flesh, we melt it in a large quantity of oil and pour it in through a straight-bored horn joined, in the manner of a clyster, [500] to a pig's bladder; we also use for this the so-called pus-drawers (pyulci). Of these too, those with a wider bore are serviceable for such a purpose. It is evident that we make a foul sinus clean by using the drug less diluted, that is, mixing it with less oil, and a clean one by using it more moistened through the admixture of more plentiful oil. If, then, there should be some suspicion of a slight inflammation still mixed in with the sinus, let the drug by all means be melted in rose oil. But if the sinus is free of inflammation, let it be melted in oil; and if it tolerates the admixture of old oil without being bitten, let the drug be dissolved in that. Suitable for such use is not only this drug but also that of Machairion and the isis, and all the others which my predecessors have written become flesh-producing for hollow ulcers when mixed with cerate.

raw_text: {"translation": "Of this same kind as cedar oil [569] is also the so-called percolated lye. And of this lye itself, the one that is made from a fine-particled material when it has been burnt surpasses cedar oil in potency. raw_text: {"translation": "It has been said in what precedes that the austere quality is necessary for malignant ulcers, and especially [771] when they are fluxional. With all these, then, that I have mentioned were mixed litharge, resin and frankincense, so that the drug might become plaster-like. But litharge belongs to the intermediate material, while frankincense is concoctive and pus-producing, if we look to the well-tempered nature. For it was shown that in moister bodies it is flesh-producing. It was also shown that none of the concoctive drugs, which indeed also possess the power called suppurative, is strongly discutient, just as none is acrid either. For such drugs heat moderately, and moreover soften rather than dry. In those books, then, from the beginning of the first book, I directed my argument against those who sophistically do away, so far as they can, with the claim of compound drugs, and who also abusively attack some of the simple ones as well, at the same time mocking those who have written about them, to the effect that some benefit the liver, others the spleen, others the kidneys or bladder or head or lung. For, they say, does someone stand over them and give them orders, as in the tragedy: 'You, go to the streams of Inachus; and you, march about Cadmean Thebes'?

For if the ecchymoses are astringed further, they become hard to disperse.

raw_text: {"translation": "But it is no wonder that Thessalus, being inexperienced in the works of the medical art and unable to discover the conditions by reason, is ignorant of everything concerning the cures of inflammations. You, however, who have often observed the most evident benefit, in many conditions, both of this phoinikinē and of other drugs compounded from opposite powers, must yourselves also attempt, whenever at some time you lack [394] those already compounded, to compound drugs according to the same method from what is readily available in that place. raw_text: {"translation": "For the patient was a boy, the son of a farmer, about fifteen years of age. Having given him as much of this plaster [403] as I had with me, to be applied, I myself returned to the city and, being taken up with a great many medical engagements, forgot about the one who had received the drug. But after two months he came back healthy, although I had not at all expected this to happen. For when we let a pig's bristle down through the little fistula, it appeared to go in as far as the articulation. By chance, a few days later, another little boy was shown to me, of the same age as the previous one and having a similar condition; I applied the plaster, and it happened that this one too was completely healed. raw_text: {"translation": "For when the wax has been added together with the resin to the white lead and the litharge, which have been boiled beforehand, until the drug becomes completely non-soiling, you would then have a white plaster, if you wish, sometimes adding water to it, sometimes oil alone, and of this oil sometimes [412] new, sometimes old. For you have already heard what power water and old oil have. You also know that both omphacine oil and the oil cultivated in Iberia, which they now call Hispania, impart something of astringency to the drug. raw_text: {"translation": "I, however, have very often prepared the drug even without water, and it appears to turn out better for all other purposes, except in those with soft skin. For in these the one that has taken up water is better, and especially when [448] the ulcers are slightly inflamed. Along with the white plasters already mentioned, Asclepiades also describes another, which promises to treat those bitten by a rabid animal, just as the one recorded by Heras also carried this promise. response.translation: [458] GALEN, ON THE COMPOSITION OF DRUGS BY KIND, BOOK II. Since the present treatise has, among its other aims, this one as well, that if we should ever lose the book in which we keep the compounding of the drugs we use written down, we ourselves should be able to compound drugs closely resembling those that are lost, it is necessary, first, that we have learned in general some outline of a way by which we shall find what we have set before ourselves.

secondly, to have been trained in this [459] way on many particular cases, knowing that without having gone through such training none of the tasks is carried out correctly. Terrible, too, is what has already befallen certain people, two physicians whom I know. For the one, wasting away from grief at the loss of such writings, died, and the other withdrew from medical practice. Those who have been trained in the way I describe have, besides being able to compound useful drugs, also the capacity to be critical judges of what was written by the physicians before us, and to make suitable use both of everything written by them and of whatever one discovers oneself according to the method that is going to be taught. It is better, then, to use those already tested through experience, once one has learned the method of their use; but, as I said, necessity often overtakes us, so that we also use untried ones, improvising. In the book before this one, then, it has been stated how one might prepare plasters from litharge alone, mixing in sometimes oil alone, and sometimes vinegar or wine or some of these, and from what proportion of them a white plaster can be produced when properly boiled.

response.translation: For when the dogmatists, asked for the reasoning by which each of the drugs they use is compounded, have nothing to say, and, having lost their written formulas, are unable to improvise other compoundings, they are themselves rightly despised, and they make the Empiricists [464] bolder in contradiction. But if they understood the nature of each affection that they treat, and knew a method such that from it they could discover both the aim of the treatment and the power of each of the simple drugs, they would not be ignorant of the reasoning of compounding. For instance, let it be proposed to consider how one would cure a hollow ulcer that is uncomplicated (for there is no harm in our also naming it so, as some call it, for the sake of concise teaching), as though no drug suitable for it had yet been found. For, having been taught by reason that the healing of hollow ulcers comes about when other flesh is generated in place of that which has been destroyed, sprouting evidently from the underlying flesh itself, we have realised that this cannot come about while there is filth in the ulcer or much moisture present. But the detergent drugs remove the filth, and the drying ones disperse the moisture.

raw_text: {"translation": "It is necessary, then, to know the materials of such drugs, not simply by kind, as Dioscorides wrote in another way, but as we did in our works on simple drugs, [465] where we wrote not only that this particular drug heats or cools or produces some other such effect, but also that it is a drug of that kind in the first remove from the mean, or the second, or the third, or the fourth. And often, too, we wrote that it is so at the middle of each of these, or at its beginning, or at its end, so that there are twelve ranks of the drugs named according to any predominance whatever. For sometimes we need a drug that heats or dries moderately, and sometimes one able to do either of these most intensely. But the man who knows only, in a general way, that the part needs to be heated will choose pepper and mustard no more readily than frankincense. These things have been said by us before, and they have also been said in the third book of the Therapeutic Method. raw_text: {"translation": "Since it was shown that ulcers which are to be filled with flesh need a drug that dries and cleanses moderately without biting, we must recall what the material of such drugs [466] is. It has been set out in the treatise On the Power of Simple Drugs, together with a statement of the rank appropriate to each. For this, as I said, is the most useful thing: that if ever one needs a stronger drug, one knows what to pass on to; and when none of the simples is at hand, we come to the compound. First, then, let it be supposed that we have wax and verdigris, but nothing else of the things directly suited to a hollow ulcer, by which I mean frankincense, iris and birthwort, meal of bitter vetch, root of panax, and all other such things. We know, then, that if wax alone is applied the ulcer will be found foul, since wax can neither cleanse nor dry, whereas if verdigris is applied the ulcer will be bitten and eroded and will become inflamed. We shall therefore decline each of these and make from both together another drug, intermediate between them, weaker than verdigris but stronger than wax. But since wax falls a little short of what could usefully be applied, while verdigris exceeds it by much, we shall mix a little verdigris with much wax. raw_text: {"translation": "[467] For this is what must be stated next: that it is not possible to find out exactly the quantity of each before trial, but it is possible to make a conjecture, to judge, and to compose at the first attempt a drug that will have no failure worth mentioning. I once did just this in a certain village, where I myself had no drug accompanying me, nor was any other of the people there supplied with one, and I found, of the things suitable for a composition, only verdigris and wax. Taking both, and melting the wax over a fire together with rose-oil so that a liquid cerate was produced, I mixed with the pound of cerate one ounce of verdigris, that is, the twelfth part. response.translation: These, then, are the drugs that Andromachus wrote down, [486] noteworthy drugs for those who know how to use them. But since they are of this kind, one must select from them those composed of fewer or more readily obtainable simples, those that are more polychrest, and those that keep most closely to the aim proposed. What I mean would become clearer with an example. Let the example, then, be a hollow ulcer, uncomplicated, in a healthy body. Such an ulcer will be treated by the so-called simple green plaster, melted together with rose-oil. They call 'simple' the one made of verdigris, wax and resin. I, as I said, mix an equal amount of each of the two, and of verdigris a tenth, or a twelfth, or an eighth. Clearly it is a twelfth if we mix a pound of wax and a pound of resin with two ounces of verdigris; and a tenth if with the two ounces of verdigris we mix twenty of both together, the resin and the wax, that is, ten of each. And indeed, even if we mix an eighth part of verdigris into the cerate made of wax and resin, that too will be well. For such a drug will be more acrid and more detergent, yet certainly not useless; for it will be suitably applied to hard bodies.

[487] A finer composition will result if one mixes an eighth part of verdigris into the composition made with wax and resin, having first ground the verdigris for several days with the most acrid vinegar. It would be finer still if we were also to mix in frankincense, a half part relative to the verdigris. Of oil you will mix in, when you prepare the drug without vinegar and frankincense, as many cyathi as there are ounces of verdigris. But when you mix in frankincense and vinegar, if the roasted [resin] is somewhat fattier and softer and you are preparing it in summer, you will mix in none; but when it is hard, and in winter, one cyathus. It is also possible for you, if you mix one of the liquid resins with the wax, to need no oil at all. Of the most liquid you will mix in a third of the weight of the wax, and of the less liquid one a half. Such a composition, clearly, will come about as follows: having melted and cooled the wax and the resin, mix them with a part of verdigris, sometimes an eighth, sometimes a tenth, sometimes a twelfth, recognising that for hard bodies the first proportion is suitable, for soft ones the third, and for intermediate ones the intermediate.

Of the wax, the pitch and the resin, twice as much as of each of those, that is, two pounds of each, must be melted with the pound of oil and so mixed with the ingredients triturated with the vinegar. This one can both conglutinate large wounds and cleanse the foul among ulcers. When cerate is added to it as it melts, it can make flesh grow. Before being melted it can also heal the thick-lipped among ulcers, press down sinuses, and in general disperse and repel.

And the green plaster written next after it is of similar power and use, having this proportion: ℞ terebinth, 1 mina; the herb serapias, 25 dr.; scraped verdigris, 10 dr.; calf's suet, 25 dr.; wax, 25 dr.; frankincense, 12 dr.; oil of cypros for the dry ingredients. And the plaster called Isis by the others he himself wrote without this name, thus: Green plaster of Epigonus. Although everyone records it, I shall nonetheless write here too the proportion of its simple drugs according to this man, since some disagree about them. For he directs one to put in burnt copper, ammoniac salt, flakes of copper, verdigris, ammoniac incense, birthwort and frankincense, an equal amount of each, 8 dr., that is 1 oz.; and of aloes, myrrh and galbanum one and a half times these, of each, that is 1½ oz., which is the same as saying 12 [dr.?] and a half; of round alum, 6 dr. raw_text: {"translation": "Those of them, however, for which the claim is greater are polychrest. [504] Some do not have many claims, but one noteworthy one: either to be suitable for the malignant among ulcers, or to disperse pus or melicerides, or to soften indurations, or some other such thing among the conditions that are neither to be despised nor easily treated. Andromachus, then, wrote down fourteen quince-yellow plasters, of which five contain verdigris, while the others have been made without verdigris. Of those containing verdigris, one is the first written of the fourteen, another the fourth, and after it a certain sixth, and after that the seventh and the tenth. All those, then, to which he has added nothing special in writing both agglutinate ulcers and cicatrise them. And, if one wishes, when melted with rose oil they also fill hollows with flesh. raw_text: {"translation": "It is an emollient (malagma); it disperses phymata, parotid swellings, scrofulous swellings (choirades), and all indurations [512], and it also works for fissures and condylomata; it is very good. Rx: litharge, 100 dr.; old oil, 100 dr.; dry pine resin, 50 or 100 dr.; wax, 50 dr. Boil the litharge and the oil until the mixture begins to draw together, and add the resin ground smooth, and when this has melted, the wax. When it is right, pour it out into a mortar previously smeared with oil, and having worked it up by rubbing, take it up. It is adhesive and does not soil. That of Hygieinus (?), of good colour, for many purposes, working on sores that are hard to cicatrize and on paronychias. There is no finer plaster than this. raw_text: {"translation": "and of the most acrid vinegar [520] 2 litrai. The metallic substances are these three: scale of black copper, verdigris and chalcitis, an equal weight of each, 2 ounces apiece, which is sixteen drachmas. When the oil is old and thick because of its age, you should put in four and a half litrai; I have once put in even 5, and I put that amount in for this reason, that it was winter. For we know that more oil is put in in winter than in summer. You will, of course, first boil the litharge to a viscid consistency. If you also have castor oil, put it in instead of the old oil. raw_text: {"translation": "A cephalic troche of the triple mixture (trimigma), effective in fractures of the head and for [545] phymata and fistulas, podagra, callosities (pōroi), ischiadic affections. Take: of red earth 2 minas (other [copies]: 12); of scale of red copper 4 minas; of Pontic isinglass 4 minas; but in the books of Heras 1 mina is found. Grind fine the red earth and the scale separately, then, together, pour in sharp vinegar so that it has the thickness of honey, and triturate; and as they dry out, pour in vinegar. For it has received this name not because it itself produces flesh or makes the parts grow together, nor as though these were not the works of nature alone, but because, when such drugs are applied, ulcers fill with flesh and grow together. Their proper work is to render the affected part free of superfluities, so that its ichors may not hinder the production of flesh or the agglutination. It was shown that the drugs that make parts grow together are more drying than the flesh-producing ones, and that the flesh-producing ones are of a detergent faculty that is least biting, whereas the agglutinative ones are not necessarily detergent at all, but need only be drying.

response.translation: It is clear, then, that being of this kind it will not incarnate the ulcer nor fill up the hollow of the flesh, but will both melt it down and diminish it; and for this reason the drugs that cleanse much filth [554], about which I spoke earlier, are not always able to incarnate, but only when, having been melted either with a larger quantity of oil or with rose oil, as are both the 'oily' drug and the one made with papyrus, the vehemence of their detergent action is curbed, or when through the admixture of cerate they become non-biting. Many of the polychrest remedies are of this kind, such as that of Machairion and the Isis. Now the aim of each of these has been stated in the books of the Therapeutic Method; and as for the material of the remedies, the simple material was stated earlier in another treatise, and the compound is stated in the present one. And first of all in it one must bear in mind the nature of the bodies being treated. Those that are moist, and for this reason soft, such as those of women and small children, and of eunuchs and of those who live in a womanish manner, require weaker drugs; but those of men, and especially of all who through manly activities and the sun have acquired a hard habit of body, are not benefited at all by the weak ones.

What I left off saying is this: that what needs to be dried does not simply need what dries, but needs it with the appropriate measure. What has advanced into much moisture needs what dries very strongly; what has advanced into little moisture needs what does this slightly; just as what has advanced into much moisture needs what dries greatly, yet not extremely nor to the utmost. raw_text: {"translation": "As I was saying, then, by mixing with the wax whichever of the resins you wish, you can bring the simple cerate, which we compound from oil and wax [591] alone, to a more adhesive consistency. raw_text: {"translation": "For all these touch the skin, [599] those of them that are in the hands and the feet being quite firmly grown together with it, whereas those that reach down to the kneecap come away from the surrounding skin by flaying. This too befell me by chance. For I devised the treatment of the nerve-wounded while I was still young, when I first returned from Alexandria to my native city, having reached my twenty-eighth year. response.translation: But rarely a little more or less than that. If, then, it ever appears oilier and moister, one must recognise that the cerate that will be made from wax melted in oil will be moister than it would otherwise be. And likewise also the one that is moderate in consistency. Pitch preserves the consistency of the cerate. As I said, the best for such a mixture is the oily kind, just as with resin too. If you put in a liquid resin, such as terebinth is in consistency, its amount should properly be a third part of the wax; and of terebinth itself, the fresh is much moister than the old.

raw_text: {"translation": "For once it has been soothed in this way, it is possible to return again to the combative course of treatment. I at any rate, when on one occasion a nerve-wounded part had been unbandaged, [633] seeing the wound irritated, and there happening to be at hand a liquid drug, the ear-remedy made with fats, warmed it in a double vessel and applied it over the affected part, and I saw a very rapid benefit arise from it, by the very perception of the patient; for he at once became free of pain, and afterwards, when we unbandaged it, it appeared to be in its natural state. [On the drug composed with pigeons' dung.] The dung of pigeons in country towers is pungent, and I once used it in the countryside for a young man with a nerve wound. raw_text: {"translation": "It is therefore safer to use them washed, since most of the bodies which we are obliged to treat [662] have at least some one condition that does not tolerate strong biting. You have heard these things many times, but now too I shall remind you of them again, and I shall ask you to keep them in mind for the whole of the discussion that follows. All bodies, then, that are plethoric, and all that are cacochymic, and in addition to these those that are soft-fleshed and highly sensitive, are readily brought into inflammation when bitten. Included among the soft-fleshed are, evidently, the bodies of white women and those of children and eunuchs and of men white in complexion, and those who inhabit a cold land: the bodies of these too are moist and phlegmatic, and for this reason soft and white. raw_text: {"translation": "Let this, then, also be added to the account: in the treatment of such ulcers, if it should be [671] possible, without harm to the whole body, for the patient to go unbathed, being rubbed down at some length with linen cloths, and next with oil, and then exercising with jumping-weights, if the affected part is a leg, or by running in the case of the parts lying above. response.translation: For all such things are hard to pulverise [678], just as those that come from dried juices or saps are easy to pulverise: myrrh, aloe, acacia and whatever is of the same genus as these. And at the end of the written recipe of the drug described above Asclepiades did well to add, in these very words: 'and unbind these every other day and foment, and having washed off the same small plaster, soften it and apply it again.' For unless the drug stays in contact with the skin for a longer time, it will accomplish nothing. This very point too has escaped most physicians, and they think that if they wipe away the ichors of the ulcer three times a day, they are doing something better than those who wipe them off twice. And those who unbind the dressing only once are often blamed by the patients themselves for neglecting them. But here too you ought to remember what we have often said in many of our treatises, that the qualities of all bodies that lie near one another act in some degree upon one another, even if one of them is much the stronger. For by this reasoning they become in time somehow of the same kind as one another, even if they differ very greatly.

raw_text: {"translation": "And when the quality of the drug has become of like kind with the body being treated, a greater benefit [679] follows. For these reasons, then, the man who first conceived of using the flat spread that had been applied before would justly be praised, and it is fitting for us to follow him all the more, since we have learned that the idea is also attested by experience. Reasonably, too, he orders that it be fomented every third day, evidently at each unbinding; for since the drug is strong, it reasonably needs soothing. It is better, then, in cases that are not very malignant, for the wax to be fourfold or fivefold the two metallic ingredients taken together. raw_text: {"translation": "For the whole affected part, and each of its parts, appears either drier or moister or hotter [687] or colder than before. In addition one should examine whether any part of the lips has been reduced, or has become in some way softened or thinned, and should also look at the alteration in colour and at the quantity of the filth. From these you will know whether a stronger or a milder drug should be applied, or the same as the first. You will also be able easily to modify the first drug itself. If you wish to make it milder, mix in, while softening it, a little of one of the astringent oils: myrtle-oil, rose-oil, quince-oil, lentisk-oil, mastic-oil or oil of cypros. If you wish to make it stronger, mix in either the scale or the verdigris. response.translation: The scale, however, is a stronger, more roughening and more biting drug, and for this reason the composer of the drug mixed in litharge, being wary of [689] the violence of the scale and wishing to relax it by the admixture of the softer drug. And if one should mix the four without wax in the stated proportion, he will have a dry dusting-powder drug that is not contemptible for the cure of malignant ulcers. But if you wish to make a plaster, it is necessary to mix in the wax as well. And because of the quantity of the metallic substances, Andromachus of necessity also mentioned liquids in the preparation under discussion, namely rose oil and myrtle oil. For the wax is very little in relation to the quantity of the metallic substances. Where, then, he directs that chrysocolla, scale and diphryges be mixed at two drachmas each of those named, and litharge at eight, plainly making fourteen in all, he needed either to mix in a very large amount of greasy wax or to add to the drug some of the oily substances. In the previously mentioned drug, by contrast, the wax was four times the metallic substances. It is therefore open to us to remove the litharge and compose the drug from the others, as I myself once did. For if one does this, he will not need the myrtle oil, since the wax, as I said, is greasy.

But if [690] it should be hard, it will be necessary to add something of the liquids as well. It is for this reason, then, that some, it seems to me, have also in such drugs added a qualification to the wax, some writing 'new', others 'fresh'. They were not, by Zeus, requiring its age, as in the case of other drugs, but its moistness. For new wax is indeed better, but not so much that one should already shun wax two or three years old. It is time to go on to the plaster written next after this one, which runs as follows. ℞ Diphryges, 84 dr.; litharge, 240 dr.; wax, 318 dr.; oil, 6 cotylae. This drug would be cicatrizing, for ulcers not yet malignant but already hard-to-cicatrise. For it dries, but not strongly, as does the one written after it. Nor, indeed, is it fitting to prepare it in so large a quantity. For this is the same as it: ℞ Diphryges, 14 dr.; litharge, 40 dr.; wax, 53 dr.; myrtle oil, 10 ounces. For the amounts written by Andromachus are sixfold of these. This, then, is truly cicatrizing, similar to the one made with cadmia and to the one called the Sweet [plaster], about which we shall speak in the following book.

raw_text: {"translation": "At any rate, since one hundred and four drachmas had been gathered together from the metallic drugs, it would have been possible [706] to mix still more of the frankincense with them; and the drug would have become milder by as much as more had been mixed in. But since he wished to keep it strong, he mixed in less. You, however, may compound it in two ways. raw_text: {"translation": "It is clear that I said that each of the others which I went through earlier benefits such ulcers, and that I grind them, compounding such drugs with the wax, for each [723] of the intractable ulcers that I treat. For sometimes I take up chrysocolla in wax, sometimes burnt copper or the scale, and this either of steel or of iron or of copper; sometimes verdigris, unburnt or burnt, as also misy and chalcitis. And occasionally I also mix in one of the astringents, about which I spoke earlier, when I wish to repel what flows in; among these are alum, pomegranate rinds and the gall, the cytini and the balaustion, and all other such things. Trusting me, then, that of all the drugs mentioned up to this point none is to be discarded, practise the method of their use, so that you may succeed as I do. raw_text: {"translation": "[On putrefying ulcers and spreading ulcers.] For putrefying ulcers and spreading ulcers (νομαί): bitter-vetch meal, liquid alum, the inside of bread made from fine wheat flour (σεμιδαλίτης), unwashed flesh of old pork or of some other old salted meat, liquid terebinth resin, [732] good honey; work equal weights together and apply. Or equal amounts of birthwort and of the juice of castor-oil-plant leaves, half as much verdigris, with water; smear it on at the thickness of honey, adding a little of the liquid. If the eschar does not come away, mix in elaterium equal to the verdigris. Sory, finely ground and sprinkled on thickly with dry lint on top, works well for putrefactions. Or anoint round about with equal amounts of round birthwort and oak-gall with oil. raw_text: {"translation": "Prepare in the usual way. The black [plaster] called 'the one with pyrites' [740], of Damonicus. It acts on fluxional, hard-to-heal and phagedaenic [ulcers]. Inserted, it also acts on fistulas, and it softens every hardness. ♃ Of litharge and asphalt, 100 or 50 dr. each; of pitch and wax, 8 dr. each; of pyrites and terebinth, 25 dr. each; of propolis and split alum, 15 dr. each; of ammoniac incense, 12 dr.; of galbanum and aloe, 8 dr. each; of verdigris and manna, 5 dr. each; of old oil, 2 sextarii. response.translation: Having ground the dry ingredients fine, leave them in the mortar; melt the wax with the oil and pour it [752] over the triturated ingredients, and let them soak it up for a short time; then add 1 kotyle of vinegar, and grind smooth for 3 days, adding as much vinegar as it will take, so that it comes to the consistency of a liquid cerate. Use it for every wound, for old and hard-to-cicatrise ulcers, and for those that are cancerous, with lint. Over the compress one should bind on lightly unwashed (greasy) wool soaked in wine and oil, undoing it every 2 days in summer and every three in winter, and wash the ulcers with lukewarm water. In deep wounds, lightly pack the openings themselves with lint; for the drug's property is that of a lint-applied remedy and pus-producing. When the ulcers have become clean and the eschar has fallen off, mix in wax equal to the verdigris and bring them to cicatrisation. It also expels carbuncles painlessly, and it arrests and heals completely every spreading malignant lesion. Use it also for herpes and for rotten nails. Likewise, for all of these one must use the wine and oil with the wool; and fill decayed teeth with the drug. Plaster of Galen. A fine one, our own.

response.translation: Moreover, in calling it the plaster of Epigonus he also disagrees with many, who, I believe, have written more accurately about Epigonus, both on other matters and on how, having been shut up in prison [776] and having healed one of the very powerful men, he was released on that account. They say that he added the root of dracontium to the drug written above, and I too have always used it in this way, since one of my teachers also used it so, putting 8 dr. of dracontium into the proportion written by Heras. Moreover, he put in half a cyathus of the oil and 1 cotyle of vinegar, and he also put in the Colophonian resin, not, as Heras did, the terebinth. He also differed from Heras in the preparation of the plaster, working up the galbanum with the vinegar together with the other ingredients in a mortar. Having mixed these, just as Heras too says, with the meltable ingredients, he then softened the drug, kneading it for a very long time in his hands while applying the sharpest vinegar. After this he placed it in a bronze vessel and, having poured [vinegar] over it, kept it for a considerable time, and only then took it out and used it. He called it, as some others also do, the plaster of Hermon the sacred scribe. In other authors you may find it written that this one too comes from the inner sanctuaries at the temple of Hephaestus in Egypt, just like the plaster with dittany.

raw_text: {"translation": "[777] The proportion of the simple drugs that compose it, however, almost all have recorded as the same, so that even if the title is different, you should not suppose that the sacred one from the inner sanctuaries, the one of Hermon the sacred scribe, and the one of Epigonus are each a different plaster. For it is called by all these names. Melted with liquid cerate it cleanses out and cicatrizes ulcers. Some have written that it should be diluted with three times as much cerate, others with double, both parties having fixed the proportion without qualification. raw_text: {"translation": "The [785] [plaster] of the Azanite. ℞ Dry pitch, 1 oz.; wax, 3 oz.; pig's fat, 3 oz.; bull's fat, 3 oz.; oesypum, 3 oz.; pine resin, 5 oz. It is effective against all malignant [conditions], gangrenes, fistulas, fresh wounds, burns, and chillings, as an acopon. It is also an emollient pessary. It is suitable too for ulcers in the uterus, for phymata, and for parotid swellings. When the ulcers are hollow, use more of the drug; when [it is applied] for cicatrization, less. It is a peculiarity of the drug that it produces a dirty crust. It is also effective in those suffering from ophthalmia, when applied on the eyelids. Oil is antipathetic to the drug; therefore guard against it. response.translation: For whereas Heraclides puts in eight drachmas of each [813] of these, Heras took six of each of them. And in Asclepiades, in the second book of the External [remedies], everything is written in fourfold proportion relative to Heras, with the further point that twelve kotylai of omphacine oil are written, Crito having written two choes. And yet his composition had everything doubled, which is why some seem to me to have added two kotylai in writing. But this in turn conflicts still more with the truth and with the text of both the Tarentine and Heras. For Heras wrote 180 drachmas, reducing the oil to weight, not to measure, on the basis that the kotyle weighs 60 drachmas. And indeed the Attic kotyle does weigh this, being a kotyle of nine Italian ounces. For the nine Italian ounces, those on the graduated horns, weigh seven and a half ounces by weight, which come to 60 drachmas, since one ounce contains eight drachmas. So in this respect too Heras agrees with Heraclides, putting in three kotylai, while Asclepiades has written twelve, since everything in his composition is written at four times the amount.

It is also effective for dysenteric patients when infused with rose oil. But when, he says, on being infused in dysenteric patients it produces a biting sensation, the spreading ulcer is to be suspected. The composition is as follows. ℞ burnt papyrus, burnt lead, and burnt and washed copper, orpiment, flake of steel, an equal amount of each; sulphur untouched by fire, half that amount. Use finely ground, either with honey or with rose oil. Moschion's, for spreading ulcers. ℞ elaterium, 2 drachms; burnt papyrus, 2 drachms; copper flake, two drachms; orpiment, 4 drachms; worm verdigris, 1 drachm; ammoniac salt, one drachm. raw_text: {"translation": "[869] [Plaster with squill.] Next after this one Criton wrote down another plaster of the same power in kind, in these very words: ℞ chalcitis, round birthwort, of each 30 dr. (others, 15 dr.); iris, 30 dr. (others, 15 dr.); dry pine resin, 30 dr. (others, 15 dr.); ammoniac, 15 dr.; myrrh, 15 dr.; storax, 15 dr.; flake of red copper, 15 dr.; roasted squill, 108 dr. Pound in the sharpest vinegar for 40 days, in the heats under the Dog-star. First the flake and the storax, a little of each of them at a time; then add the ammoniac and the copper and the squill, so that it may be thoroughly worked; then the resin, a little at a time; after these the myrrh; then, when these are smooth, the remaining dry ingredients. raw_text: {"translation": "Reasonably, then, in the drug before us, although its aim is to heat and to dry and for this reason also to produce psydraces [pustules], something of the astringents too was mixed in. But since these two, chalcanthum and salt, are not sufficient against many violently heating drugs, copper flake too was mixed in by the same [877] reasoning, and so was alum, which also took this very name because it astringes violently. Another. Crito recorded another, very celebrated plaster, which he names the Mesian. Its material is of a different kind from that of the plaster written above, and from that of the one I am about to write next, which Crito himself names the invincible and which is composed mostly of acrid drugs. The Mesian is not of this sort, as will be shown later at its own proper occasion. Moreover, he also names certain others 'cephalic', whose general property will be stated a little later. For he did not make clear of how many ounces of the Roman litra he means the kotyle to be. And yet it would have been better for one who had lived in Rome to mention litrai, xestai and ounces, and to leave aside the name of the kotyle, which is in use in the Greek cities outside Italy. Now if the name of the kotyle denoted the same thing in all of them, there would be no question. But as it is, since there is a very great difference in quantity among them, he ought to have said either 'I mean the Attic kotyle', or the Alexandrian, or the Ephesian, or some other. Most of those who have written on measures and weights say that the kotyle written by physicians in pharmacological books is one of 9 ounces of the Roman litra. Others say that the kotyle meant by them is the one of 12 ounces, just as in Rome they customarily give the name 'litra' to the litra of oil.

response.translation: The drug before us, then, has been found to be powerfully discutient, so that it is able to disperse even pus already formed, at least when it is not very much, without perforating the skin; and to be emollient of parts that are becoming scirrhous and of those hardened in any way whatever; and agglutinative of large wounds, just as it is also cicatrizing of ulcers that have already turned malignant, [901] and of all the other affections that are measured by (? μετρεῖται) a faculty at once discutient and repellent. Among these are also the applications placed on the forehead for eyes suffering from flux, which physicians call anakollēmata. This same drug will also be suitable for nerves that have been laid bare, even if they happen to have been cut in some part of them. For nerves that have been cut right through no longer carry the danger that arises from sympathy, and they also take away sensation from the bodies lying beneath them, into which they are distributed (? κατίσχεται). Yet these too need a drug of this kind. For moistening drugs readily putrefy them. For this reason the drying little discs too, although they are considerably astringent, nevertheless suit nerves that have been laid bare, at least those that have not yet arrived at the peak of the inflammation. For these are irritated and exacerbated by such drugs. But these matters will be discussed as the account proceeds; concerning the plaster before us, let us add to the account what remains.

raw_text: {"translation": "When it thickens, add the pitch [915] and the verdigris, then ladanum and the galbanum, and having poured it out in this way into a mortar, knead it and use it. Some, so that it may become of good colour and grey, also mix in 8 drachms of scale; for otherwise it becomes very black. I have often used this one also for gout, and it worked excellently. One should use pine-splinters instead of logs. It is plain that the men disagree slightly in the other ingredients, but very greatly in the proportion of the oil; for Andromachus puts in double what Heras does. Now, however, I shall describe the plasters that have already given sufficient proof in trial, saying only this much more about them: that some have also mixed some of the astringent drugs into the attractive ones, guarding against what happens in those cases in which there will be a surplus of humours.

Then, taking it off, sprinkle in 1 ounce of root of wild cucumber, 4 ounces of root of xiphion, and 4 ounces of flower of Assian stone. Another, of Antipater. Take: 1 pound of nitre, 1 pound of terebinth, 1 pound of old oil, 1 xestes of water, and more. When, as it boils, it no longer bubbles up, add 2 ounces of ammoniac incense, 1 ounce of galbanum, 1 ounce of bdellium, 2 ounces of frankincense, 2 ounces of sandarach, and 2 ounces of Assian stone. The Assian stone and the sandarach are ground smooth with a little oil; the meltable ingredients are scraped up and mixed with the dry ones. Another discutient, of Antipater. Take: 300 drachms of molybdaena, 150 drachms of wax, 30 drachms of terebinth, 6 drachms of chalcitis, 8 drachms of galbanum, 8 drachms of myrrh, 8 drachms of manna, and of oil 4 kotylai in winter, 3 kotylai in summer. Another, of Xenocrates, anodyne, discutient, as Castus gives it, the plaster of Polystomus for gouts. Take: 150 drachms of white lead, 3 pounds of wax, 30 drachms of terebinth, 30 drachms of aphronitre, and 3 kotylai of old oil. Another discutient, for meliceris, of Alexander. Take: 1 pound of Spanish salt, 1 pound of litharge.

raw_text: {"translation": "And we see many who, from erysipelases that were immoderately subjected to these [i.e. strongly cooling and astringent applications], have scirrhous [994] swellings, through the ignorance of the physicians who treated them. The first difference, then, between the drugs that treat inflammations and those that treat scirrhi is the one that has been stated. Another is the difference arising from the pain conjoined with inflamed parts, which does not tolerate a strong drug being applied to the affected part. response.translation: Of malabathrum unguent, [1024] 1 pound; of sampsuchum, 1 pound. Cutting the roots into thick pieces, and putting them together with the sampsuchum into the oil, and setting it over coals, boil; and when the roots have dried out, squeeze out the liquid, and throw away the roots and the sampsuchum. Then, letting the frogs down into a little woven basket, sewing up its lips, and putting it into the squeezed-out oil, set the vessel back on the fire, covered with a lid. When a sufficient interval has passed for the frogs to have melted away, lift out the basket, squeeze out the liquid, and throw the basket away. To the oil that remains add the meltable ingredients, stirring continually. Last of all add the marrow and the galbanum; and when it has dissolved, lift it from the fire and let it cool somewhat, then sprinkle on the dry ingredients, pounded and sifted through a very fine sieve, stirring continually; and having emptied it into a mortar and pounded it, add 1½ pounds of malabathrum unguent. Pound again, take it up into a leaden vessel, and keep it airtight. The drug is to be used sometimes as a malagma (emollient), once the abatement of the disease has set in, and sometimes also as an ointment for rubbing on.

response.translation: Put it into a small perfumer's vessel made of tin, cover it [1044] carefully with a lid, and leave it for twelve days and twelve nights. Let the must be made ready at the same time, from grapes cleanly pressed out, so that it contains nothing of dew. Then, putting the must into a large bronze cauldron, so that there is room also for the boiling-up of the must, add all the ingredients that have been soaked in the wine, together with the oil and the wine; and let it be stirred twice a day with a perfumer's spatula for an hour. Let the spatula be wiped carefully, so that what has remained on it and turned sour may not spoil the drug when the spatula is put in again. Let the vessel be fitted with a lid and, above, with several piercings (κεντρῶσι), and let it be tied round carefully. Let a coiled ring be placed under the vessel. When fifteen days have passed, let the ammoniac and the amomum itself be added, pounded rather coarsely. At thirty days one must give it two or three boilings in a double vessel over coals, adding the opobalsam to the unguent as well. Then, taking the vessel off and letting it cool for a while, pour off the unguent.

response.translation: But if you wish to make it more efficacious [1058] for the conditions I mentioned before, add four drachms of Atlantic euphorbium. For in this way it will be pleasant and active, even though it is composed of few ingredients. I have known some, however, who use many fats, and much marrow, and certain aromatics, and juices, and unguents, and certain oils; having in turn made use of these myself, I came, of course, to recognise that such things belong to men lacking in taste, who have not discerned the ingredients and the simple natures of these.
